turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll take your observations before you go in. Sleeve up there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, grand. Is it much longer? The head is pounding and I've been clock-watching outside.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): He's nearly ready. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, temperature thirty-six point seven, oxygen ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one thirty-eight bad? Could the blood pressure be what's driving the headache?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Only mildly up. The doctor will go through it. In you go.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit down. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The headaches. I've had migraine for years, but it's changed, and I'm really frightened about it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Changed how?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse in the morning. I wake up and it's already pounding, the whole head, and I've been getting sick with it.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A month at least. I'm awake with him from about five.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not a month. It's a fortnight, two weeks. I'm nearly certain.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll call it a few weeks and not fight over the day. Vomiting every morning?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not every morning. Only a few times. I can't tell you when the vomiting started, it crept in, maybe last week, I genuinely don't know.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in an arm or a leg?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. If I did get weakness, what would that mean? Should I be checking?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): It would mean the emergency department. Speech slurred? Seeing double?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Speech is normal and there's no double vision.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stiff neck?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the neck is fine.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He snores the house down as well, and he's tired all day. Asleep on the couch after the tea.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not snore. She's exaggerating. And I'm not tired. I'm grand once the headache lifts.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do snore, loud, most nights, and you are tired. I've watched it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not having that row in here. Can we stay on the headache? I was googling tumours half the night.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the migraines been there?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Since my twenties. I'm forty-two, so about twenty years. My dad had migraines too, the same sort of thing.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, when one starts. I've been taking it nearly every day lately, which is too much, and that worries me as well.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box at home says a hundred milligrams. He keeps telling people fifty.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought it was fifty. Maybe the chemist changed it. I haven't checked the new box, so I can't swear to the dose.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else for the pain?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two of the five-hundred milligram tablets, maybe three if it's desperate, most days. Is that dangerous? Could it be causing the morning headache?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Daily paracetamol can keep a headache going. Were you on a preventer?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Propranolol, forty milligrams twice a day. I stopped it in March, it had me wrecked. They offered topiramate after and I never took a single capsule.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): This might sound stupid, but my sister takes biotin every day for her hair. Would it help if I tried some? She also wants me to ask about her mother's tablets.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My mother takes metformin for her diabetes. I only wondered if that kind of thing did anything for headaches.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. The biotin is your sister's and the metformin is her mother's. Neither is yours. Anything else you're on?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else. So do I stop the paracetamol today? Am I allowed any sumatriptan at all?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut the paracetamol right back, not every day. Keep the sumatriptan for a proper attack, not every morning. I'll have a look at you.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pupils are equal and reacting to light. There's no swelling at the back of the eyes.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the pressure thing, isn't it? So that's clear? Does that mean I'm alright?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): It makes very high pressure less likely. It doesn't close it. Power is normal in both arms and both legs, and the reflexes are present.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Coordination is fine, finger to nose is accurate. No neck stiffness. Your gait is steady.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you think it actually is? Don't soften it, please.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is a change in the migraine, with medication overuse likely on top. I wouldn't rule out raised pressure, given the morning vomiting.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're scanning me today, then?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it hasn't settled in two weeks, or the vomiting gets worse, we might arrange a brain scan.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Might, so it's not booked. If I wake up worse on Sunday, do I just wait?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): New weakness, confusion, or a sudden terrible headache, you go to emergency, you don't wait. Otherwise I'll see you in a fortnight.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if I feel a bit better? And would the scan be an MRI or a CT? I'm awful in tight spaces.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): The fortnight visit stands either way. If we do a scan it would be an MRI, and only if things haven't settled. Nothing is booked for imaging today.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the two-week review in the book at the desk. Mornings are easier.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning, please. Is there anything else I should watch for, or am I overthinking it?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting that won't stop, confusion, a thunderclap headache. Don't start the biotin, and leave the metformin alone.
[SEG0054] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And you're not going to touch the snoring at all?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): There is no snoring, and I am not exhausted. I wish you'd drop it.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sleep can wait. Emergency if anything sudden happens. Otherwise two weeks.

spec.situation: Person with long headaches who now has a different pattern (worse in the morning, or with vomiting); takes sumatriptan or paracetamol often; partner says snoring and tiredness too; patient dismisses it. Doctor does a quick neuro exam and orders a scan conditionally.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

omissions.text: Sumatriptan dose was stated by the patient as 50 mg when one starts, though this was disputed by the family member who said the box says 100 mg; the actual dose remains unconfirmed. The recorded medication entry omits the stated 50 mg dose.
Propranolol was stopped in March because it made the patient feel 'wrecked'.
Topiramate was offered after propranolol, but the patient never took a single capsule.
Headache location/character detail: the patient said the headache is 'pounding' and involves the whole head.
Negative finding from examination omitted: finger-to-nose testing was accurate.
Doctor explicitly said imaging is not booked today / not scanning today.
Planned follow-up was specifically a two-week review in the morning if possible, with the nurse booking it.
Additional red-flag advice not fully captured: emergency care was advised for confusion and for a 'thunderclap headache'/'sudden terrible headache', and the doctor said not to wait if these occur.
